name: Calcium hydroxide relaxer

lead: A calcium hydroxide relaxer is the 'no-lye' alternative to the traditional sodium hydroxide cream, used to permanently straighten tightly curled hair. The straightening is visible right after treatment, and it is often marketed toward people with sensitive scalps.

Calcium hydroxide is mixed at the time of use with a guanidine carbonate activator, producing guanidine hydroxide, a weaker alkali that breaks the hair's disulfide bonds. Only treated hair changes; new growth keeps its natural texture. Available health studies do not separate calcium-based products from lye ones.

paras: It is mixed just before use and applied like other relaxers, at a salon or at home, then rinsed and neutralized. People repeat it on new growth as their natural texture comes in.
Burns, dermatitis and breakage are reported for both lye and no-lye relaxers. Observational health studies have not separated product types, and cosmetics are not pre-approved by the FDA.

angle.text: Calcium hydroxide 'no-lye' relaxers mix with an activator to form guanidine hydroxide, which loosens curl bonds and permanently straightens tight curls, visible right after treatment. They are marketed as an option for sensitive scalps, though studies have not shown a different health profile from lye relaxers.

lead: A calcium hydroxide relaxer, sold as a "no-lye" relaxer, is a chemical hair straightener used to turn tight curls or coils into smoother, straighter hair. Its active agent is guanidine hydroxide, formed when a calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) cream is mixed with a guanidine carbonate activating solution just before use. [1][2]

Like other relaxers, it permanently alters treated hair by breaking the disulfide bonds that hold the curl, so new growth stays curly and needs retouching. [2][2] Wikipedia describes lye relaxers as containing 5 to 10 percent sodium hydroxide at a pH of 10 to 14, and the no-lye group as milder alkalis including potassium, lithium or guanidine hydroxide; products of this kind are positioned for sensitive scalps. [1][2]

Wikipedia cautions that scalp burns can occur with lye and no-lye relaxers if the scalp is overexposed, and that contact dermatitis is possible. [1] Studies of relaxer use and health outcomes do not separate calcium-based products from sodium hydroxide ones. [1]
infobox: Guanidine hydroxide, from calcium hydroxide plus guanidine carbonate [1]

paras: The calcium hydroxide cream and guanidine carbonate activating solution are combined shortly before use, generating guanidine hydroxide, which Wikipedia describes as a weaker alkali than sodium hydroxide. [1] The alkali breaks disulfide bonds in the hair keratin similarly to lye products. [1][2]

Other no-lye approaches include potassium or lithium hydroxide, ammonium thioglycolate, which must be oxidized afterward, and ammonium sulfite or bisulfite in home kits that are weaker and slower. [1] Relaxers are generally suited to coarse, tight curls. [2]

Garrett Augustus Morgan is credited by Wikipedia with discovering a hair-straightening cream by accident in 1909. Lye relaxers went on sale in 1917, and the first commercial no-lye relaxer, using potassium hydroxide, followed in 1919. [1] Straightening was very popular in the 1950s, and Madam C. J. Walker popularized the straightening comb in the early 1900s. [2]
In the 1990s the Rio Hair Naturalizer System, marketed as chemical-free, was associated with scalp damage and hair loss, led to a class action and was withdrawn. [1]

Both lye and no-lye relaxers can cause scalp burns, irritant or allergic dermatitis and hair breakage. A petroleum-jelly base is often applied to the scalp beforehand. [1] No separate risk profile for calcium hydroxide products is given. [1]

Wikipedia also reports health studies on relaxer use generally: a 2012 cohort of more than 22,000 African-American women found an association with uterine fibroids, a 2022 NIH analysis of more than 33,000 women reported nearly doubled uterine cancer risk among frequent users of hair-straightening products, and a 2017 study found women using chemical relaxers were nearly twice as likely to develop breast cancer. [1][2] In 2023 the FDA proposed banning formaldehyde as a relaxer ingredient. [1] These studies did not analyse by alkali type. [1]
No studies specific to calcium hydroxide relaxers were identified. Studies of relaxer use generally, described above, did not compare the two alkali types. [1]
